routes.claim: A periodic quarter-wave stack of TiO2 and SiO2 can be tuned to reflect the visible band while transmitting NIR, provided the layer thicknesses are adjusted to compensate for the blue shift at 45 degrees incidence.
transfer_assumptions: The blue shift observed in the source (normal to 60 deg) applies qualitatively to the 45-degree case, requiring a red-shifted design target.
TiO2/SiO2 index contrast is sufficient to create a broad enough stopband to cover 450-650 nm with a moderate number of layers.
Unpolarized performance is approximated by the average of s and p responses, which may broaden the effective edge but reduce peak reflectivity compared to single polarization.

routes.claim: Optimizing the thickness ratio of high-to-low index layers away from the standard quarter-wave condition can improve unpolarized performance at oblique incidence by balancing s- and p-polarization stopbands.
transfer_assumptions: At oblique incidence, the effective optical thickness differs for s- and p-polarizations, causing their stopbands to split.
A standard quarter-wave design optimized for normal incidence will suffer from this splitting at 45 degrees, reducing the common high-reflection bandwidth for unpolarized light.
Adjusting the physical thickness ratio dH/dL can partially re-align the s and p stopbands or maximize their overlap in the visible region.

routes.model_knowledge_rationale: Retrieved evidence confirms angular dependence and blue shift but does not provide specific thickness ratios for optimizing unpolarized TiO2/SiO2 stacks at 45 degrees. This route relies on general thin-film physics: at oblique incidence, the admittance of s and p polarizations diverges. A standard quarter-wave stack (optical thickness = lambda/4) designed for normal incidence will have mismatched phase conditions for s and p waves at 45 degrees, leading to split stopbands. By empirically adjusting the physical thickness of the high-index layer (dH) while keeping dL constant (or vice versa), one attempts to find a compromise thickness that maximizes the constructive interference overlap for both polarizations in the target visible band. This is a heuristic optimization strategy common in filter design when exact analytic solutions for unpolarized oblique incidence are complex.
